answers.answer: Starlette is a Python ASGI framework/toolkit for asynchronous web services: HTTP, WebSockets, lifecycle handling, middleware, responses and optional integrations. Application developers import it and supply routes/endpoints. An external ASGI server runs the resulting callable; the README demonstrates uvicorn main:app. Components can also be embedded independently in other ASGI applications. Tests invoke applications in-process through TestClient. This repository is the library, not the server's socket/HTTP parser.

Principal runtime package starlette/: applications.py composes application state and middleware; routing.py dispatches routes; convertors.py defines typed URL conversions; requests.py exposes HTTP scope/body/form APIs; responses.py serializes and sends responses, including JSON, streams and files; websockets.py manages message/state transitions; middleware/ provides composable cross-cutting wrappers. staticfiles.py serves directories/packages, templating.py integrates Jinja2, and background.py/concurrency.py run tasks and bridge synchronous work. tests/ contains pytest behavior tests and fixtures; scripts/ drives checks, coverage and tests; docs/ contains user guidance; pyproject.toml defines packaging and tool configuration.

A single declared Python distribution, starlette, uses Hatchling (hatchling.build), with its version read from starlette/__init__.py and Python >=3.11. Runtime boundaries are ASGI callable/message contracts and the starlette modules; the server and application endpoints are external. Required dependencies are AnyIO >=4,<5 and conditional typing_extensions for Python <3.13. The full extra includes Jinja2, multipart, sessions/signing, YAML, telemetry and HTTP clients. TestClient prefers httpx2, with deprecated httpx fallback. uv manages dev/docs groups; pytest/coverage, Ruff and strict mypy provide checks. Documentation is Markdown/HTML with Zensical/mkdocstrings dependencies, shell scripts automate checks, and the debugger embeds HTML/CSS/JavaScript. No compiled-extension build is established by these inspected files.

Construction is Starlette(routes=...), which creates Router. Runtime public-library entry is Starlette.__call__(scope, receive, send): it puts the application into scope['app'], lazily builds/caches middleware_stack, then awaits that stack. The ASGI server supplies the scope and receive/send callables. Parsing TCP/HTTP bytes into that scope is an external boundary, not implemented at this entry point. If lifespan ran first, the stack can already exist when the first HTTP request arrives.

routing.compile_path resolves ':int' through CONVERTOR_TYPES and builds the named regex capture. Route.__init__ stores the compiled result; Route.matches extracts groups and invokes convert(). convertors.IntegerConvertor supplies [0-9]+ and int(value); the registry maps 'int' to its instance.

build_middleware_stack -> Middleware descriptors for ServerErrorMiddleware, optional RequestBodyLimitMiddleware, and ExceptionMiddleware; it also consumes self.user_middleware and self.router. Proof is executable construction at applications.py L67-L74, not imports alone: descriptors are iterated into cls/args/kwargs, then cls(app, ...) wraps the previous app. Middleware.__iter__ proves that unpacking direction. The Router instance was created by __init__, not by this method. Effective outside-in order: ServerError -> optional body limit -> configured user middleware -> ExceptionMiddleware -> Router. 500/Exception handlers go to ServerError; other handlers go to ExceptionMiddleware. __call__ -> build_middleware_stack is the incoming edge. Custom middleware classes remain runtime-supplied targets.

For an unmounted route with no custom middleware: server -> Starlette.__call__ -> ServerErrorMiddleware -> ExceptionMiddleware -> Router.__call__/app -> route.matches -> FULL/child-scope merge -> route.handle -> request_response adapter -> int_convertor(Request) -> JSONResponse -> ASGI send. Matching/conversion is detailed in q5/q10. The synchronous test endpoint runs through run_in_threadpool -> AnyIO. Exception wrappers surround the downstream calls. Dynamic boundaries: server, ordered configured routes, middleware/endpoint callables, convertor registry, AnyIO scheduler, receive/send. This is a source-derived path, not an executed trace.

Evidenced direct consumers: BaseRoute.__call__ uses self.matches for standalone routes; Router.app calls route.matches in both normal dispatch and slash-redirect probing. These are polymorphic calls resolving to Route.matches for Route instances. Changing match classifications or child_scope can affect endpoint selection, parameters, 404/405 and redirects. Exact failures, downstream applications and uninspected/custom callers remain speculative; no exhaustive whole-repository caller claim is made.

tests/test_routing.py::test_route_converters performs client.get('/int/5'), asserts status 200 and JSON {'int': 5}, and separately checks reverse URL generation. Its client fixture wraps the module-level Router containing the integer Route, not a Starlette instance. test_client_factory returns a backend-configured TestClient; its HTTP transport builds the scope and calls the app through an AnyIO portal, entering the Router dispatch described above. Thus this is an integration test of integer conversion and endpoint output, not a direct unit call to IntegerConvertor.convert.

In production the external server supplies scope['path']='/int/5'; in the test, _TestClientTransport reads request.url.path and sets scope['path']=unquote(path), separately retaining raw_path bytes. get_route_path reads path and handles root_path. The route regex captures param='5'; Route.matches calls IntegerConvertor.convert('5') -> int('5') -> 5, then returns child_scope.path_params. Router merges that scope. Request.path_params exposes the stored mapping; int_convertor reads ['param'] and returns JSON {'int': 5}. The endpoint receives a Request, not a separately injected integer argument. raw_path and the request body are not the conversion input.
